title: Gauge Pressure, Absolute Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
lead: A tire gauge on a flat tire reads zero although the air inside it is at atmospheric pressure, because gauges are built to read zero there. This section defines gauge pressure as the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure and absolute pressure as the total, relates the two, and then looks at the instruments that measure pressure: the aneroid gauge, whose bellows turn a pressure into a force and a force into a reading; the open-tube manometer, which reads a gauge pressure as the height of a column of fluid; the mercury manometer of a blood pressure cuff; and the barometer, which reads the atmosphere itself.
objectives: Define gauge pressure and absolute pressure.
Understand the working of aneroid and open-tube barometers.
summary_html:
• Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure.
  • Absolute pressure is the sum of gauge pressure and atmospheric pressure.
  • Aneroid gauge measures pressure using a bellows-and-spring arrangement connected to the pointer of a calibrated scale.
  • Open-tube manometers have U-shaped tubes and one end is always open. It is used to measure pressure.
  • A mercury barometer is a device that measures atmospheric pressure.

figures.original_caption: This aneroid gauge utilizes flexible bellows connected to a mechanical indicator to measure pressure.

An open-tube manometer has one side open to the atmosphere. (a) Fluid depth must be the same on both sides, or the pressure each side exerts at the bottom will be unequal and there will be flow from the deeper side. (b) A positive gauge pressure P_g = hρg transmitted to one side of the manometer can support a column of fluid of height h. (c) Similarly, atmospheric pressure is greater than a negative gauge pressure P_g by an amount hρg. The jar’s rigidity prevents atmospheric pressure from being transmitted to the peanuts.

In routine blood pressure measurements, an inflatable cuff is placed on the upper arm at the same level as the heart. Blood flow is detected just below the cuff, and corresponding pressures are transmitted to a mercury-filled manometer. (credit: U.S. Army photo by Spc. Micah E. Clare\4TH BCT)

A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure. The pressure due to the mercury’s weight, hρg, equals atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is able to force mercury in the tube to a height h because the pressure above the mercury is zero.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the fluid reaches equal levels on either side of a manometer if both sides are open to the atmosphere, even if the tubes are of different diameters.

answer.solution: The pressure at a point in the fluid is due to the weight of the fluid above it and to the atmosphere pressing on the surface, $\kPr = \kPatm + \kh\krho\kg$, and it depends on the depth alone, not on the amount of fluid or the width of the tube above the point. Take a point at the bottom of the U, where the two sides meet. The atmosphere pushes down on both open surfaces equally, so if the fluid stood higher on one side, the pressure at the bottom from that side would be greater by the extra depth times $\krho\kg$, and the fluid would flow away from the deeper side until the depths were equal. A wider tube holds more fluid, but the pressure at a depth is the same in a wide tube and a narrow one, so the diameters make no difference to where the levels come to rest.

exercises.prompt: Figure 11.15 shows how a common measurement of arterial blood pressure is made. Is there any effect on the measured pressure if the manometer is lowered? What is the effect of raising the arm above the shoulder? What is the effect of placing the cuff on the upper leg with the person standing? Explain your answers in terms of pressure created by the weight of a fluid.

answer.solution: The cuff is connected to the manometer by air, whose density is so small that the pressure due to its weight over a height of a meter or so is negligible, so lowering or raising the manometer itself has no effect on the reading: the pressure in the cuff is transmitted to the mercury undiminished wherever the manometer sits. The blood in the arm is another matter, because blood is a liquid about as dense as water. Raising the arm above the shoulder lifts the artery in the arm above the heart, and the pressure there is lower than at the heart by $\kh\krho\kg$ for the height raised, so the cuff reads a lower pressure. Placing the cuff on the upper leg of a standing person puts the artery well below the heart, and the pressure there is greater than at the heart by $\kh\krho\kg$ for that depth, so the reading is higher, as the problem set works out for a cuff 0.500 m below the heart. This is why the cuff is placed on the upper arm at the level of the heart.

exercises.prompt: Considering the magnitude of typical arterial blood pressures, why are mercury rather than water manometers used for these measurements?

answer.solution: A manometer reads a gauge pressure as the height of a column of fluid, $\kPg = \kh\krho\kg$, so the height for a given pressure is $\kh = \kPg/\krho\kg$ and is inversely proportional to the density of the fluid. A typical systolic pressure of 120 mm Hg raises mercury only 120 mm, which fits in a tube that stands on a desk or hangs on a wall. Water is 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so the same pressure would raise a column of water 13.6 times as high, about 1.6 m, and the problem set finds that a water manometer for pressures up to 300 mm Hg would have to be 4.08 m tall. A mercury manometer is compact enough to use and to read, and a water manometer for blood pressure is not.

exercises.prompt: Find the gauge and absolute pressures in the balloon and peanut jar shown in Figure 11.14, assuming the manometer connected to the balloon uses water whereas the manometer connected to the jar contains mercury. Express in units of centimeters of water for the balloon and millimeters of mercury for the jar, taking $\kh = 0.0500\ \text{m}$ for each.

parts.hint: In a water manometer the gauge pressure is the height of the water column itself when it is written in centimeters of water, and the balloon holds the column up on the open side.
Atmospheric pressure in the same unit is in Table 11.2, and the absolute pressure is the gauge pressure added to it.
The jar is below atmospheric pressure, so its gauge pressure is negative, and in a mercury manometer it is the height of the mercury column in millimeters.
Table 11.2 gives one atmosphere in millimeters of mercury; take the jar’s gauge pressure away from it.

exercises.prompt: How tall must a water-filled manometer be to measure blood pressures as high as 300 mm Hg?

answer.hint: Convert 300 mm Hg to pascals with $1.0\ \text{mm Hg} = 133\ \text{Pa}$, then find the height of water that makes that pressure from $\kh = \kPg/\krho\kg$.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you measure a standing person’s blood pressure by placing the cuff on his leg 0.500 m below the heart. Calculate the pressure you would observe (in units of mm Hg) if the pressure at the heart were 120 over 80 mm Hg. Assume that there is no loss of pressure due to resistance in the circulatory system (a reasonable assumption, since major arteries are large).

parts.hint: The extra pressure is that of a column of blood 0.500 m tall, $\kh\krho\kg$ with the density of blood, converted to millimeters of mercury.
Add the increase to the 120 mm Hg at the heart.
Add the same increase to the 80 mm Hg at the heart.

answer.solution: $\kdPr = 38.7\ \text{mm Hg}$, so the blood pressure at the leg is $\dfrac{159}{119}$.

exercises.prompt: Assuming bicycle tires are perfectly flexible and support the weight of bicycle and rider by pressure alone, calculate the total area of the tires in contact with the ground. The bicycle plus rider has a mass of 80.0 kg, and the gauge pressure in the tires is $3.50\times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$.

answer.hint: The tires hold the weight $m\kg$ up with a force equal to the pressure times the area of contact, and it is the gauge pressure that does it, because the atmosphere presses on the outside of the tire and on the ground alike.
